clips.send: Someone who just got handed a tube of antibiotic ointment for a cut sends this to a friend with the same tube in their cabinet: the thing the doctor wasn't allowed to say out loud - the anger of being handed the second-best option by law.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau cut his finger on a cigar cutter and ended up in the ER. The doctor bandaged it and told him to use Neosporin or Bacitracin - standard orders.

Then he asked about manuka honey instead. She told him, quietly, it works better and faster than what she's allowed to prescribe - her license only lets her recommend approved drugs, never a food.

He used the honey anyway. Five days later, at the follow-up, the cut was 99% closed - the progress the ointment usually takes two full weeks to reach.

She never got to say it on the record. He's saying it for her.

Ever had a doctor tell you something 'off the books'?

clips.send: Someone who's failed every 'total overhaul' diet sends this to the friend about to try again: the version that starts with just one apple - the relief of not having to change everything at once.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says most people fail at 'getting healthy' because they try to change everything on day one.

His actual advice to a friend who wanted in: don't take anything out yet. Just add one organic apple a day for a week or two. Nothing else changes.

Next, add a half-gallon of pure spring water a day - no tea, no flavoring, just water. He says that's step one; step two is working up to a full gallon later.

Small adds, not a full overhaul - that's the whole method.

What's the one thing you'd add first?

clips.end_words: don't put it on your skin
clips.send: Someone who just grabbed a drugstore body spray sends this to the friend who reads every food label but never flips the lotion bottle over: the same rule applies to both - the anxiety of realizing what's been soaking into their skin for years.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau's rule for anything you put on your body: if you wouldn't eat it, don't put it on your skin either.

Whatever touches your skin gets absorbed into your bloodstream, he says - it's the same reason drug companies deliver medicine through skin patches instead of pills. The skin is a fast way in.

So he points to the label on most full-body deodorants: 'not for human consumption, if ingested call poison control.' If it's dangerous to swallow, he asks, why is it fine to rub into your skin every day?

Next time you reach for a lotion or spray, flip it over and read what it actually says.
